150.t: Palace Theater big bands and the Natchez fire
150.s: He and friends heard big bands at the Palace Theater and Tick Tock, and he tells how a lack of money kept them from a Natchez show that burned.
150.ch: After high school: riverfront and tailoring
150.q: Well, yes, because it was a style at the time. John McNeely, Charles Dimes, myself, Edward Johnson, we were all good friends. And we all would meet down on Rampart Street and we'd party at the Pelican or sometime we went to the Tick Tock. We used to go to the, see, then we'd go to the Palace…

150.t: 1940s touring acts: Erskine Hawkins, Wynonie Harris, Andy Kirk with Big June Richmond
150.s: Stephens recalls 1949 shows by Erskine Hawkins, Mabel Scott, Gatemouth Brown and blues concerts at the Dewdrop and Foster's, then Andy Kirk's 1942 visit; the tape is paused.
150.q: We left off. Yeah, well let's fill in where we left off. Let's go back to the 40s and we'll update things. Some of the things we didn't cover, like when Oyskin Hawkins came here in 1949. He played at the Booker T. Washington Auditorium. And incidentally, Mabel Scott played at Foster's Rainbow Room,…

150.t: Andy Kirk, Pha Terrell, Mary Lou Williams and top 1940s venues; Eddie Vinson
150.s: Stephens restarts with Andy Kirk's 1942 visit, Mary Lou Williams at the Coliseum and Gypsy Tea Room, lists the top venues, and praises Eddie Cleanhead Vinson's blues singing.
150.q: Well, Ted, you know, we left off talking about moving into a new era into the 70s, 80s, before we got into the 90s, getting a little backdrop on history. A lot of things that we discovered on the tapes that we have been doing. Let's backdrop a little bit. Let's go back to the 40s, back in 1942,…

371.t: Billy Eckstine's band at the Cotton Club and Fats Navarro falling through the stage
371.s: A single engagement with Eckstine's band; Jones tells how Navarro jumped from the top tier and fell through the floor.
371.q: It’s possible. I don't recall it. He was great on valve trombone, like Bobby Brookmeyer. He was very inventive, he had great tone, great sound, and a great jazz style. You know, valve trombone has a different sound than regular slide trombone. But, it has a throaty field. But, it's sound is great…

224.t: Joining Luis Russell: Savoy, Apollo and the band's people
224.s: He recalls the singer Lee Richardson, trombonist Emery Thompson and his own drum feature.
224.ch: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
224.q: The thing about it, I had a feeling to want to play with a big band right after, and that thing came right on time, to go to New York. I started at the Savoy Ballroom with him, and the Apollo Theater, and all those places.

100.t: Lou Terrassi's club, Hot Lips Page collapsing and big-band stage shows
100.s: Hearing Roy Eldridge, Charlie Shavers and Joe Thomas near the Times, Page fainting on a high note, Tommy Dorsey, and Basie with Billie Holiday before the draft.
100.ch: Greenwich Village, Central Plaza and the Times
100.q: on drums, whom I knew. That’s how I first met Roy. Charlie Shavers had a great little group there. That was when [Hot] Lips [Page] sat in with Charlie. I remember they played Royal Garden Blues. Lips hit a high note and passed out. He just slid down. He was leaning against a wall at the bandstand,…

90.t: Big bands at the Michigan and Paradise theatres
90.s: Seeing Sinatra with Dorsey and the Black bands, including Basie, Hines with Eckstine and Sarah Vaughan, at the Paradise.
90.q: There was plenty of good listening around the city during that period. I remember going down to the Michigan Theatre. That's where I first heard Frank Sinatra with the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra. That was a real treat. And Timmy Rogers was on the bill, the comedian and musician; he was on the bill.…

385.t: Joining the Cats and the Fiddle; the Apollo
385.s: Snags Allen turned down the guitar job and recommended him; the group, with its hit I Miss You So, played the Apollo, close behind the Ink Spots.
385.ch: California, Cats and the Fiddle, the Tatum trio
385.q: That part I don't know. But the thing of it is they offered it to Snags, the same guy I was talkin' about. And somehow or other he didn't want to leave town or he had something, I forgot. Anyhow, he referred me. And I really gave 'em an audition, in a way of speaking. They say we gonna get together…

235.t: Claude Hopkins at the new Zanzibar with Nat King Cole's trio
235.s: With Claude Hopkins and lead altoist George James he played for Bill Robinson and on Nat Cole's first New York engagement.
235.ch: Back in New York: Heard and Dizzy
235.q: No, he had a trio. He was a star. He was on stage. That was a great experience, being with Claude Hopkins. You know I've seen him several times years later. I even got J.J. Johnson to do I think it was a couple of things for the band. Claude Hopkins bought music all the time. Yeah, sure. You know…

81.t: Claude Hopkins compared with Andy Razaf
81.s: Hopkins was sedate and well trained with a big band at the Cotton Club, while Razaf was loaded with talent; Johnson collaborated with both.
81.q: Oh, gosh, it's like night and day. Claude is more sedate and light, and yet and still he's down there -- with Andy, it looks like Andy had more talent than he knew what to do with. He was just loaded with talent. There were so many different things he was... (inaudible), he was terrific, Razaf was.…

171.t: Luis Russell's weak band with Lil Green, Gatemouth Moore and the Ink Spots
171.s: Russell's band had few real soloists but backed Lil Green and Gatemouth Moore on packages from Moe Gale's office.
171.ch: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
171.q: And because most of the guys he had in there were -- few were pure amateurs with the exception of Holmes and another alto player that had been -- I think he went blind or something. Then he had -- kept Jesse Powell, who was a beginner, learner. He didn't even know how to take a solo, couldn't play…

79.t: Claude Hopkins's band and Babe singing with him
79.s: Thomas spent a year or more with Claude Hopkins at Roseland. Babe recalls working with him at the last Uptown Cotton Club show and the Howard, and Joe describes his slow comedy.
79.q: Babe was a personality on her own. She was a feature performer with Lunceford, the Harlem Express, a feature performer. ... Hop, I guess it might have been a year and one-half but he was a tremendous person, tremendous musician. Lot of comedy.
